params.prompt: Priya signs the group health contract for her bakery. That document is the master policy, and Priya, the employer, is the policyholder. Her employees are not parties to the contract. Each covered employee receives a certificate of coverage, sometimes called a certificate of insurance or evidence of coverage, describing the benefits, exclusions, cost sharing and how to file a claim. The certificate is a summary; the master policy controls if they differ. Dependents are covered through the employee’s certificate. When a question asks who the insured is in group coverage, the answer is the employee; who owns the policy, the employer.

Because the certificate is all most employees ever see, Maryland and federal law require it to be accurate and complete. It must describe the benefits and limitations, the conditions for eligibility, how coverage ends and the continuation and conversion rights that follow. Maryland’s continuation statutes specifically require each certificate to explain how a surviving spouse, a divorced spouse or a terminated employee may elect continued coverage. The Affordable Care Act added the summary of benefits and coverage, a standardized four-page comparison document. A certificate that misstates benefits exposes the insurer to claims for the benefits described.

How is the group’s premium set? Experience rating bases next year’s premium on this group’s own claims history, adjusted for trend and expenses; it is used for large groups whose claims are statistically credible. Community rating charges all groups in an area the same rate regardless of claims. Federal and Maryland law now require modified community rating for small employers: premiums may vary only by age within a three to one band, tobacco use, geographic rating area and family composition, never by the group’s health or claims. Priya’s twenty-person bakery is community rated; a two thousand-employee hospital is experience rated.

Group insurance works because the group formed for some purpose other than buying insurance. Employees come together to work, union members to bargain, borrowers to borrow. That natural purpose means the group’s health is roughly average and no one joined because they were sick. A group assembled solely to buy insurance would attract the people who most need it, defeating the pricing. State laws therefore define the eligible groups, require a minimum size in some cases, and in Maryland permit true small employers down to a single eligible employee through the small group market and S H O P.

Employer groups cover the employees of a single employer, the most common form. Creditor groups cover borrowers; the lender is policyholder and the coverage pays the debt, as in credit disability. Labor unions cover members, often through trusts the union and employers fund jointly. Multiple employer trusts pool small employers, usually in the same industry, so they can buy coverage on better terms; Maryland regulates these multiple employer welfare arrangements closely because some have failed. Associations formed for purposes other than insurance, typically professional or trade associations in existence for at least two years, may cover members. Credit unions cover their members.

When a question names an organization, ask two things. Was it formed for a purpose other than insurance? A trade association that has existed for years and happens to offer a health plan qualifies; a club organized last month to get cheap insurance does not. Who holds the master policy and who receives certificates? In an employer group it is the employer and employees; in a creditor group, the lender and borrowers; in an association, the association and members. Then ask how the premium is set: by the group’s own experience if large, by modified community rating if it is a small employer.

Theo markets a group plan to Priya and then helps her explain it to employees. The same truth-in-advertising rules apply: materials must be accurate, name the insurer, and present limitations as clearly as benefits. Enrollment meetings, brochures and the certificate itself are advertising for this purpose, and the insurer is responsible for them. Employer communications that oversell the plan can create liability for benefits the plan does not provide. The summary of benefits and coverage uses a standard format precisely so employees can compare plans without marketing spin.

Group contracts cross state lines. The general rule is that the law of the state where the master policy is delivered governs the contract, even if certificate holders live elsewhere. An employer headquartered in Delaware with a Maryland branch may hold a Delaware master policy. Maryland protects its residents by extending certain mandated benefits and consumer protections to certificates delivered to Maryland residents under out-of-state group policies, and by requiring out-of-state carriers to be authorized here. When a question asks which state’s rules apply, start with the place of delivery, then check for extraterritorial provisions.

An insurer underwriting Priya’s bakery does not examine twenty people. It examines the group. Characteristics of the group include its size, industry, age and gender mix, location and turnover; a stable workforce in a low-hazard industry prices well. Plan design matters: rich benefits with no employee contribution invite heavier use than a plan with cost sharing. Persistency, the group’s history of staying with carriers, signals whether the insurer will recover its setup costs. Administrative capability, the employer’s ability to handle payroll deductions, enrollments and records, affects expense. For small groups, health status may not be used at all.

The insurer requires a minimum share of eligible employees to enroll. In a noncontributory plan, where the employer pays the entire premium, one hundred percent of eligible employees must participate, because there is no reason for anyone to decline. In a contributory plan, where employees pay part, carriers typically require about seventy-five percent of eligible employees who do not have other coverage to enroll. The rule prevents a plan from enrolling only the sickest employees. Priya’s plan is contributory; she needs at least fifteen of twenty eligible employees to join, not counting those covered by a spouse’s plan.

Carriers also require the employer to contribute a minimum share of the premium, commonly at least fifty percent of the employee-only cost. The contribution makes enrollment attractive to healthy employees, which keeps the risk pool balanced and the participation requirement reachable. Maryland’s small group market and the S H O P marketplace allow carriers to set reasonable participation and contribution requirements, applied uniformly, and to decline a small group that fails them, even though they may never decline for health. A small business tax credit may offset part of the employer’s share for qualifying employers that buy through S H O P.

Every rule in this lesson fights the same enemy: adverse selection. Advertising rules keep employees from buying on false expectations. Jurisdiction rules make sure a state’s protections follow its residents. Group underwriting prices the whole group fairly without singling out sick employees. Participation and contribution requirements make sure the healthy join along with the sick. Theo tells Priya that meeting the participation rule is not bureaucracy; it is what keeps her premium affordable next year. Lesson thirty-seven turns to the employees themselves: who is eligible, when they may enroll and how benefits coordinate.
